description: Module checkpoint assessment verifying mastery of learning objectives across: Introduction to SQL, Core Syntax and Primitives in SQL.

questions.prompt: [Module 1: Foundations & Core Concepts of SQL] A query filtering on WHERE UPPER(email) = 'USER@EXAMPLE.COM' is causing full table scans despite an index on email. What is the solution?

options.text: Create a functional/expression index on UPPER(email) or normalize email to lowercase before indexing and querying
Add an extra ORDER BY email ASC clause
Convert the column type from VARCHAR to TEXT
Change the SELECT clause to SELECT *

questions.explanation: Wrapping indexed columns in functions disables standard B-Tree index lookups unless an expression index exists or values are pre-normalized.

questions.prompt: [Module 1: Foundations & Core Concepts of SQL] What rows are returned by this SQL query?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

options.text: Only department IDs that have strictly more than 5 employee records
The first 5 departments ordered by employee count
All employees in departments where at least one person makes over 5k
A syntax error because WHERE was omitted

questions.explanation: HAVING filters aggregated groups after the GROUP BY clause, retaining only groups satisfying the aggregate predicate.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Syntax and Primitives in SQL

questions.prompt: [Module 1: Foundations & Core Concepts of SQL] Which of the following are ACID properties in relational database transactions?

options.text: Atomicity: All operations in the transaction succeed or all roll back
Consistency: The transaction brings the database from one valid state to another
Isolation: Concurrent execution of transactions yields the same state as serial execution
Adaptability: Schema changes apply dynamically without migration locks

questions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

questions.prompt: [Module 1: Foundations & Core Concepts of SQL] What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT OUTER JOIN?

options.text: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matches in both tables; LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves all left rows and fills unmatched right columns with NULL.
LEFT OUTER JOIN returns only unmatched rows.
INNER JOIN can only be used on primary keys.
LEFT JOIN sorts the results in ascending order automatically.

questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all records from the left-hand table regardless of whether the join predicate matches a row on the right.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Syntax and Primitives in SQL

questions.prompt: [Module 1: Foundations & Core Concepts of SQL] What will happen if you compare a column value with NULL using '=' (e.g. WHERE status = NULL)?

options.text: It returns UNKNOWN (evaluating to false in WHERE), matching zero rows; 'IS NULL' must be used instead.
It matches all rows where status is an empty string.
It triggers a syntax error in ANSI SQL.
It converts NULL to zero.

questions.explanation: In three-valued SQL logic, NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Checking for nullability requires the 'IS NULL' operator.
